| Early Years | Nurseries, pre-schools, Pre-K | Daily diary, photo moments, pickup authorization with QR/OTP, developmental milestones, nap/meal logs | Early-years observations, parent consent records, NEP Foundational stage HPC |
| K-12 Core | All schools | Admissions, class/section/house, attendance, timetable, gradebook, report cards, behaviour, homework, fees, transport, library, health | UDISE+ (India), DfE census (UK), state reporting adapters (US), CBSE/ICSE/state-board exports, PARAKH HPC |
| International / IB / Cambridge | International schools | Unit planners, MYP/DP criteria, CAS/service hours, extended essay tracking, predicted grades, university counselling, multi-currency fees | IB and Cambridge exports, transcripts, CASE standards alignment |
| Higher Education | Colleges, universities | Programme and curriculum design, CBCS/credits, semesters, electives, registration, examinations (internal/external, revaluation), results, transcripts, convocation, hostels, placements, research, alumni | ABC credit transfer, APAAR, DigiLocker/NAD, NAAC SSR/AQAR, NBA SAR (CO-PO-PSO attainment), NIRF data mart, AISHE DCF, Samarth migration |
| Coaching / Tuition | Test-prep and tuition centres | Batches, lead CRM, trial classes, instalments, test series, rank lists, doubt-clearing, franchise roll-up | GST invoices, batch performance reports |
| Vocational / Skills | ITIs, polytechnics, skill centres | Trades, practical hours, apprenticeships, competency checklists, industry partners | NCVET/skill-credential exports, Open Badges |
| Multi-Campus Group | Trusts, MATs, chains, university systems | Group dashboards, central admissions, shared staff, consolidated finance, policy templates pushed to campuses, cross-campus benchmarking | Consolidated statutory returns, group-level audit |
| Government / Ministry | State education departments, district offices | Read-only aggregated dashboards, school inspection workflows, scheme tracking (scholarships, mid-day meals, uniforms), grievance portal | Open-data exports, GIGW 3.0 accessibility, state-level UDISE+ reconciliation |

**Terminology toggle.** The same field displays as "pupil / form / Year 7" (UK), "student / homeroom / Grade 7" (US) or "student / class / section / house / Std VII" (India). It is set per tenant and per user language, so staff moving from any competitor see familiar words from day one.

## V.5 Switching-Cost Destroyers: The Migration Engine

Migration pain is the main reason institutions stay with a system they dislike (gap C6). OpenCampus One treats migration as a flagship product, not a services project.

### V.5.1 Competitor importers

Each importer ships as an open-source connector with test fixtures and a published field map.

| Source system | Import method |
|---|---|
| PowerSchool SIS | Data Export Manager CSV, PowerQuery extracts, OneRoster 1.1/1.2 CSV or REST, Universal Rostering |
| Infinite Campus | OneRoster 1.2 REST/CSV, ad hoc report CSV, ODBC extract templates (customer-run) |
| Skyward, Synergy, Aeries, Focus | OneRoster and Ed-Fi ODS, vendor CSV templates |
| FACTS, Blackbaud, Veracross, Alma, Gradelink | SKY API (Blackbaud), vendor CSV/XLSX exports, OneRoster |
| Ellucian Banner/Colleague, Anthology, Workday Student, Jenzabar, Oracle Campus Solutions | Ethos EEDM resources, flat-file extracts, Workday report-as-a-service CSV, PeopleSoft query exports |
| Arbor, Bromcom, SIMS, iSAMS | CTF/ATF (Common Transfer File, UK), census XML, vendor API/CSV, SIMS SQL export via customer-run script |
| Compass, ManageBac, Toddle, Classter | CSV/XLSX exports, OneRoster, ManageBac API |
| Indian ERPs (Fedena, Entab, Teachmint, Camu, MasterSoft, NextOS, Edunext, MyClassboard, Skolaro, Vidyalaya, Academia, OpenEduCat) | Excel/CSV templates, Fedena and OpenEduCat database adapters, UDISE+ data-capture formats, Tally XML/JSON for ledgers |
| Spreadsheets and paper | Smart Excel templates, phone-camera OCR of admission registers and mark sheets with human verification |

### V.5.2 AI-assisted mapping and data-quality report

An "Import Studio" detects the source system from file signatures and proposes column mappings with confidence scores. It runs more than 150 validation rules before anything is written: duplicate students and guardians, sibling and household inference, invalid dates, orphan enrolments, fee balances that do not reconcile, and missing UDISE/APAAR/PEN identifiers. The output is a human-readable data-quality report with one-click fixes, and the person approving the import signs it off. Mapping is deterministic and saved as a reviewable file, so it can be version-controlled and reused by the next school migrating from the same vendor.

### V.5.3 Shadow parallel-run mode

For one term the old system stays the system of record. OpenCampus One syncs nightly or in real time where APIs allow, and staff use it for attendance and communication first. A reconciliation dashboard shows any drift (attendance totals, fee balances, grades) between the two systems. Cut-over is a button press, once the drift report shows zero critical differences.

### V.5.4 Familiarity layer

The terminology toggle (V.4) works alongside "muscle-memory" navigation presets that mirror common menu structures. For example, "Gradebook → Assignments" for PowerSchool users and "Students → Registers" for SIMS users, both mapped to the same underlying pages. Grading scales, attendance codes and report-card templates import as-is: DfE attendance codes, CBSE grading, US letter grades and GPA, and IB 1–7.

### V.5.5 Exit guarantee

A one-click full export produces a signed archive. It contains all data in documented JSON, CSV, OneRoster and Ed-Fi formats, all files, the audit log and the schema documentation. It is free, unlimited and part of the licence promise, which turns the incumbents' exit fees into a sales argument.

### V.5.6 Commercial switching incentives

The hosted service charges nothing for the remaining months of a competitor contract (up to 12 months). Standard migrations are free. Certified partners offer fixed-price migrations for complex universities.

## V.7 Signature Features: Ten Ideas No Incumbent Offers Together

1. **Shadow Switch.** The parallel-run migration of V.5.3. A school trials OpenCampus One for a full term without risk, and the reconciliation report proves readiness. It addresses C6, the biggest switching barrier.
2. **Family Super-App.** One parent login covers every child at every campus, from nursery to university. It includes attendance, homework, fees through the family wallet with UPI AutoPay, bus ETA, canteen balance, consent forms, conferences and auto-translated chat. It addresses C4 and C10, where competitors force several apps.
3. **Offline Classroom Mode.** Teachers take attendance, enter marks and write behaviour notes in a basement lab with no signal. Records sync with deterministic conflict rules when the device reconnects, and offline edits are always auditable. It addresses C9.
4. **Channel Waterfall with Delivery Proof.** A message tries push, then WhatsApp, then SMS, then a voice call in the guardian's language, and stops at the first confirmed delivery. The cost of every channel is shown up front. It addresses C9 and C10.
5. **Consent Ledger (DPDP-native).** Each data purpose (admissions, photos, AI, transport tracking, APAAR) has a versioned notice in the guardian's language and verifiable parental consent with DigiLocker-token support. Withdrawal propagates to processors, and an evidence pack is ready for the Data Protection Board. It is built to the DPDP Rules 2025 phased schedule, with child-consent rules (Rules 3 and 5–16) due 18 months after the 14 November 2025 notification, around May 2027. Comparable GDPR, FERPA and COPPA packs exist for other markets. It addresses C7 and C8.
6. **Accreditation Autopilot.** The NAAC, NBA, NIRF and AISHE evidence vault fills itself from operational data, with lineage back to the source record. It replaces the spreadsheet scramble before every accreditation cycle. It addresses C5 and C8.
7. **Ask OpenCampus with Receipts.** The AI copilot answers questions such as "Which Grade 9 students have below 75% attendance and an unpaid term fee?" Every answer links to the records it used. It never acts without approval and can run fully on-premise. It addresses C11.
8. **One Learner, One Lifetime Record.** A single identity follows the learner from nursery to alumni across campuses in a group. It exports as a verifiable credential (W3C Verifiable Credentials, Open Badges 3.0, CLR) and pushes to DigiLocker/ABC. It addresses C12.
9. **Trust Center in the Product.** Each institution can see who accessed what and when, every export, every API token, every support session (just-in-time and approved by the school), and backup-restore test results. It addresses C7 and is a direct answer to the PowerSource-style support-plane breach.
10. **Leave in One Click.** A full, free, signed export in open formats at any time, written into the licence and the hosted terms. It addresses C6 and turns lock-in into a reason to choose OpenCampus One.

## V.8 UX Principles: Simple, Clean, Classic, Feature-Rich Underneath

1. **"Today" home screen per role.** A teacher sees the next class, an attendance button, unmarked work and messages. A principal sees attendance, fee collection and alerts. A parent sees each child's day. No menus are needed for the 80% of daily tasks.
2. **Command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+K) and universal search.** Type "Aarav fee" or "Grade 7B timetable" and go straight there, with typo-tolerant search.
3. **Progressive disclosure.** Simple defaults with an "Advanced" layer for power users, so the platform is easy for a 200-student school and deep enough for a 40,000-student university.
4. **Classic, calm visual language.** A neutral palette with one accent colour per institution, generous whitespace, a clear type scale (Inter or Noto Sans for Indic scripts), consistent tables, keyboard-first data entry and no visual clutter.
5. **Mobile-first for teachers and parents, desktop-optimised for office staff.** Bulk tasks such as fee posting, timetabling and exam processing get dense desktop layouts.
6. **Accessibility as a gate, not a feature.** WCAG 2.2 AA, screen-reader tested, large-touch targets, dyslexia-friendly font option, reduced motion, high contrast. GIGW 3.0 mapping for Indian government tenants.
7. **Low-bandwidth mode.** Under 200 KB per first screen, image-free option, works on 2G/3G and on low-end Android phones with 2 GB RAM.
8. **Vernacular everywhere.** The UI, notifications, report cards and voice prompts are available in the user's language, with voice input for teachers who prefer speaking to typing.
9. **Guided wizards for rare but critical tasks.** Year-end rollover, promotion, timetable generation, census and UDISE submission, and exam result publication all have a preview, an undo window and a checklist.
10. **In-product learning.** Contextual tips, 60-second videos, a sandbox copy of the institution for safe practice, and a "what changed" panel after each release.

## V.9 Technical Architecture: Lessons from the Top 3 Backends

Part IV shows what to copy and what to avoid:

- PowerSchool has deep in-process plugins and a support portal that became a breach path.
- Infinite Campus has per-customer Windows/SQL Server/Tomcat instances, an ODBC escape hatch and fragmented OneRoster versions.
- Ellucian Ethos has a strong canonical resource and event layer, but complex versioning and legacy self-service surfaces.

The blueprint architecture:

```text
                Cloudflare (DNS, CDN, WAF, TLS)  -- static PWA, docs, edge cache
                                 |
   Web PWA (SvelteKit or Next.js)  |  Mobile (Expo/React Native)  |  Desktop kiosk (Tauri, optional)
                                 |
                   API gateway (rate limits, auth, OpenAPI 3.1)
                                 |
 +-------------------------------+--------------------------------+
 | Modular monolith (TypeScript/NestJS or Python/Django)          |
 |  identity | people | admissions | academics | attendance |     |
 |  assessment | finance | HR | operations | comms | compliance  |
 +-------------------------------+--------------------------------+
        |                |                  |                |
 PostgreSQL 17 + RLS   Outbox -> queue   Object storage    Keycloak / ZITADEL
 (system of record)    (workers, webhooks, (R2 / Garage)    (OIDC, SAML, passkeys)
        |               search, notifications)
 Read replica -> analytics store (Superset, semantic layer)
        |
 Offline sync (PowerSync or Electric) -> SQLite on devices
        |
 OpenTelemetry -> Grafana / Loki / Tempo / Prometheus
 AI service (Ollama/llama.cpp local; vLLM GPU; optional cloud) via permission-aware retrieval
```

**Architecture decisions and why:**

1. **Canonical education model plus projections.** Internal entities are stable. OneRoster 1.2, Ed-Fi, CEDS, UDISE+ and DfE census are adapters with conformance tests, so no standard dictates the internal schema. This is the Ethos lesson without Ethos's licensing barrier.
2. **Modular monolith first.** It is one deployable unit with strict module boundaries, which makes it easy to self-host on a €6 VPS and to secure. Modules can be extracted to services later where load demands it. This avoids the per-customer instance sprawl visible at Infinite Campus.
3. **Multi-tenancy in the database.** Every row carries `tenant_id`, PostgreSQL row-level security enforces isolation, and the application never connects as a table owner. A dedicated-database tier is available for universities and governments that need it.
4. **Durable events.** A transactional outbox gives every event an immutable ID, tenant ID, schema version, actor, causation ID and replay window. Webhooks have retries and dead-letter queues, and connectors have reconciliation endpoints. This fixes the undocumented replay and ordering gaps seen in PowerSchool's and Ellucian's public event models.
5. **Capability-scoped plug-ins.** Plug-ins are signed manifests that declare scopes, events, UI slots and rate limits. They run out-of-process (WebAssembly sandbox or separate container) and never get database superuser access. This keeps PowerSchool-style flexibility without its blast radius.
6. **Separated planes.** The operational, integration, analytical and support planes are separate. Support staff use just-in-time, tenant-approved, time-boxed, read-only-by-default access with full audit. That is the direct lesson of the PowerSource incident.
7. **One policy-aware API for every client.** Web, mobile, partners, reports and AI all receive the same authorization decisions. There is no weaker "mobile API".
8. **Selective offline.** Attendance, mark drafts, behaviour notes, timetables and messages work offline. Fee settlement, result publication and identity changes require online confirmation.
9. **Reconciliation as a feature.** Every connector has full sync, delta sync, cursor recovery, dry run and human-readable error reports.
10. **Evidence by default.** Audit logs, export logs, token inventory, event-delivery health, dependency inventory (SBOM) and backup-restore results are visible to each tenant. There is also a public status page.

## V.10 Open-Source Stack and Licensing

| Layer | Choice | Licence | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Database | PostgreSQL 17 (+ pgvector, pg_trgm) | PostgreSQL License | RLS, JSONB, full-text search, mature operations |
| Backend | TypeScript + NestJS (alternative: Django) | MIT / BSD | Large talent pool, typed domain modules |
| Web | SvelteKit or Next.js PWA | MIT | Installable, offline caching, fast first load |
| Mobile | Expo / React Native | MIT | Shares TypeScript and UI logic; native push and camera |
| Desktop (optional) | Tauri | MIT / Apache-2.0 | Lightweight kiosk and exam-hall client |
| Offline sync | PowerSync open-source components or ElectricSQL | Apache-2.0 / MIT | PostgreSQL-aware partial replication to SQLite |
| Auth | Keycloak (alternative: ZITADEL) | Apache-2.0 | OIDC, SAML, LDAP, passkeys, multi-realm |
| Search | PostgreSQL FTS first; Meilisearch Community Edition | MIT | Typo-tolerant search; enterprise edition avoided |
| Object storage | Cloudflare R2 (hosted) or Garage (self-hosted) | Service / AGPL-3.0 (Garage) | Low egress; MinIO avoided because its community edition is frozen |
| Workflow | Outbox + workers; Temporal for long processes | MIT | Durable timers and approvals; n8n avoided (Sustainable Use License) |
| BI | Apache Superset + semantic layer | Apache-2.0 | Open dashboards on a read replica |
| Video | Jitsi Meet / BigBlueButton | Apache-2.0 / LGPL-3.0 | Self-hostable conferences and classes |
| AI | Ollama / llama.cpp, vLLM; IndicTrans2 for translation | MIT / Apache-2.0 / MIT | Local, private inference; 22 Indian languages |
| Timetabling | Google OR-Tools CP-SAT | Apache-2.0 | Proven constraint solver |
| Observability | OpenTelemetry + Grafana LGTM | Apache-2.0 / AGPL-3.0 | Portable telemetry |
| Deployment | Docker, Coolify or Dokploy; Helm charts for Kubernetes | Apache-2.0 | One-click self-hosting |

**Project licence.** The core platform is AGPL-3.0, so anyone can use, modify and self-host it for free, including commercially. Anyone offering a modified version as a network service must publish their changes, which protects the community from closed SaaS forks. SDKs, connector templates, the design system and API clients are Apache-2.0, so vendors and institutions can build proprietary integrations without copyleft concerns. Documentation is CC BY 4.0. There is no source-available bait and switch: every feature in the core stays OSI-licensed. Contributions use the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO), and the trademark is held by a non-profit foundation to protect the name.

**Licensing cautions found in this research.** n8n uses the Sustainable Use License (not OSI). MinIO's AGPL community edition is frozen, and AIStor is commercial. Meilisearch Enterprise is BUSL. The Vercel Hobby plan is for personal, non-commercial use. Open-weight AI models each carry their own licence terms. All of these are excluded from the core or flagged in the dependency policy.

## V.11 Security, Privacy and Compliance by Design

**Baseline standards.** OWASP ASVS 5.0 Level 2 for the whole application, with Level 3 for authentication, finance and the support plane. The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 ISMS and SOC 2 Type II evidence model is built into the hosted service from day one.

**Identity.** Passkeys (WebAuthn Level 3) and phishing-resistant MFA are mandatory for staff. Parents can sign in with an OTP or a passkey. Sessions are short-lived and refresh tokens rotate. Admins can revoke any device.

**Isolation.** PostgreSQL RLS is tested in CI with negative tests, and the application has no superuser connections. Each tenant gets its own encryption key (envelope encryption) for sensitive fields such as health, safeguarding, identifiers and bank details.

**Support plane.** Support access is just-in-time, approved by the institution, time-limited, reason-coded and recorded. Bulk export by support staff is impossible without dual approval. Anomaly detection runs on exports and API usage.

**Software supply chain.** Signed releases (Sigstore), SBOM per release, dependency scanning, secret scanning, SAST and DAST in CI, reproducible builds, a public vulnerability disclosure policy, a bug bounty and an annual external penetration test with a published summary.

**Data protection packs.** These are versioned and dated per jurisdiction:

- **India:** DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025 with the phased commencement correctly labelled. Verifiable parental consent, no behavioural tracking or targeted ads for children, a breach workflow with a 72-hour detail window, grievance officer tooling and retention and erasure orchestration.
- **US:** FERPA, COPPA (2025 amendments), PPRA and state student-privacy laws such as California SOPIPA.
- **EU and UK:** GDPR, UK GDPR and the Age Appropriate Design Code.
- **Australia:** Privacy Act and the Children's Online Privacy Code.

**Data residency.** The hosted service runs in-region (India, EU, UK, US) and every subprocessor is listed publicly.

**Resilience.** Encrypted off-site backups, point-in-time recovery, quarterly restore drills with results shown to tenants, RPO of 15 minutes or less and RTO of 4 hours or less on hosted plans.

## V.12 Deployment Paths: Zero Cost to Low Cost

| Path | Who | Monthly cost (estimate) | Components |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Developer and demo | Contributors, evaluators | $0 | GitHub Free (code, CI, Pages docs), Cloudflare Pages/Workers Free (PWA, docs), Neon Free or Supabase Free with synthetic data only, Cloudflare R2 free tier (10 GB) |
| Single school self-hosted | One school with an IT teacher or partner | €6–€20 | One Hetzner cloud VM (from €5.49–€5.99/month excl. VAT), Coolify or Dokploy, PostgreSQL, Garage or R2, nightly encrypted off-site backups, Cloudflare DNS/WAF free |
| School group or small college | 5–20 institutions | €25–€75 | Two VMs (app + database), R2, monitoring, separate backup target |
| Hosted SaaS by the project | Institutions that want no IT | $25–$300+ infrastructure per region | Managed PostgreSQL with replicas, autoscaled app nodes, search, observability, paid messaging |
| Government or university on-premise | Ministries, large universities | Own data centre | Helm charts on Kubernetes, air-gapped AI option, dedicated database tier |

Free tiers are used only for development, documentation, demos and public assets, never as the system of record for real student data. Oracle Cloud Always Free can host a zero-cost pilot when capacity is available, but it must have off-provider backups. WhatsApp, SMS and voice traffic, payment-gateway fees, app-store fees and GPU inference are pass-through costs shown transparently to institutions.

## V.13 Business Model, Go-to-Market and Sustainability

**Revenue model (open core without crippleware):**

1. **Hosted OpenCampus Cloud** with a public price card. Indicative targets, to be validated with pilots:
   - India: free up to 100 students, then ₹15–₹30 per student per year for schools and ₹60–₹120 for higher education.
   - UK: £2–£4 per pupil per year.
   - US private schools: $1–$2 per student per month.
   - All core modules are included in every plan.
2. **Usage pass-through** for messaging, payments and AI at cost plus a small published margin.
3. **Enterprise services** for universities and governments: dedicated tenancy, SLAs, accreditation consulting and integration projects.
4. **Certified partner network.** Local implementers in every state and country earn the migration and training revenue, which builds the support capacity that incumbents lack (C3).
5. **Marketplace revenue share** on paid community plug-ins (70/30 in favour of developers).
6. **Grants and public funding.** Digital public goods registration (Digital Public Goods Alliance), education-ministry partnerships, CSR funding for government schools and philanthropic grants for offline and low-resource features.

**Go-to-market:**

- Start with 50 lighthouse schools and 5 colleges in two Indian states (for example Telangana and Maharashtra), migrated free from Fedena, Teachmint, Entab, Excel and paper.
- Publish the case studies and the migration time for each.
- Run a "Switch Season" campaign before every academic year: April–June in India, June–August in the UK and US.
- Give government schools a free hosted tier funded by CSR and grants. This builds massive adoption (the adoption score drives 30% of the ranking) and creates a reference base for private schools.
- Build developer community through hackathons on connectors and plug-ins, and student contributors through university open-source programmes.
- Use analysts and review sites: proactively collect G2, Capterra and app-store reviews from day one, since UX/mobile ratings are where incumbents are weakest.

**Governance.** A non-profit foundation holds the trademark and roadmap. A technical steering committee includes institution representatives. Public RFCs cover major changes, with a long-term-support release every 12 months.

## V.15 Success Metrics and Key Risks

**North-star metrics:**

- Weekly active teachers and parents as a share of enrolled users
- Median migration time per institution
- Net Promoter Score by role
- App-store rating (target at least 4.6)
- Support first-response time
- Share of institutions using offline mode
- Cost per student compared with the incumbent replaced
- Security: zero cross-tenant incidents, mean time to patch critical CVEs under 72 hours

**Key risks and mitigations:**

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Scope is too broad for a new team | Strict phase gates; the school MVP must replace an incumbent for one segment before HE work begins |
| Open-source sustainability | Hosted revenue, partner network, grants and foundation governance; AGPL protects against closed forks |
| Incumbent response (price cuts, bundling) | Compete on exit freedom, offline, compliance and transparency, which closed vendors cannot match quickly |
| Regulatory change (DPDP rules, state laws) | Dated policy packs with a public change log; legal review per release |
| Security of a public codebase | Defence in depth, bug bounty, signed releases and external audits; openness speeds discovery and fixes |
| AI errors or bias | Retrieval with citations, human approval, bias monitoring, admin kill switch, no autonomous high-stakes decisions |

## V.16 Projected Position Against the Ranked Platforms

Applying the same rubric to the planned capabilities at the end of Phase 4 gives this result. It is a design target, not a measured result.

| Dimension | Weight | Target score | Basis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Feature breadth | 30% | 10 | All modules in V.6 across K-12 and higher education; segment packs |
| Adoption | 30% | 6 (year 3) to 9 (year 5) | Free core plus government-school programme plus switching engine |
| Advanced features | 20% | 10 | Permission-aware copilot, early warning, auto-timetabler, accreditation autopilot, verifiable credentials |
| UX and mobile | 10% | 10 | Offline-first apps, Today screens, accessibility, vernacular |
| Interoperability | 10% | 10 | OneRoster 1.2, LTI 1.3, Ed-Fi, CASE, Open Badges, UDISE+, ABC, DigiLocker, open API and events, one-click exit |
| **Weighted** | | **8.8 (year 3) to 9.7 (year 5)** | Year 3 already ties PowerSchool's 8.8; year 5 would rank #1 worldwide and in India |

The decisive factor is adoption, which carries 30% of the score. That is why the plan pairs a free open-source core with a migration engine and a government-school programme: features alone will not win the ranking unless institutions can switch easily.

# Appendix A. Interoperability, Privacy, Accessibility, Security and India DPI Requirements

**As-of date: 27 November 2026.** This report translates the named standards, laws, regulatory programmes and Indian education platforms into product requirements for an open-source school, college and university management platform. “Must support” means either a legal/customer procurement obligation in the relevant market or a practical integration requirement. A standard is not itself a law: conformance, certification, contract terms and local education-sector rules still have to be checked for each deployment.

### How to design for the whole market

The platform should separate a canonical education data model from adapters and policy controls. The canonical model should cover people, organisations, courses, classes, enrolments, attendance, assessments, results, credentials, competencies, staff, facilities, fees and audit events. Every field needs provenance, effective dates, source-system identifiers, sensitivity classification, retention rule and a data-sharing purpose. Adapters should expose REST/JSON, CSV and event interfaces, preserve external identifiers, support idempotent upserts, and keep an append-only interoperability/audit ledger.

The product should have tenant- and jurisdiction-level policy packs rather than one global default. A US K–12 tenant needs FERPA/COPPA/PPRA and state-contract controls; an EU or UK tenant needs GDPR-style rights, international-transfer and child-design controls; an Indian tenant needs DPDP controls plus UDISE+, APAAR, DigiLocker/NAD, ABC, DIKSHA and regulator reporting. Accessibility, security, consent, retention, breach and export functions must be built into the core rather than bolted on to each connector.

A useful release and procurement rule is: implement the base specification, publish versioned API documentation and test fixtures, then obtain a certification where a market or buyer values it. 1EdTech says its standards are free to download and use, but claiming conformance requires membership and completion of the relevant certification process. [1]

### Interoperability standards

| Standard | What it is and who uses or requires it | Concrete platform implications |
|---|---|---|
| **1EdTech OneRoster 1.2** | A school-ecosystem exchange standard. It securely exchanges users, organisations, courses, enrolments, classes, resources, gradebook line items/results and assessment results between SIS, LMS and learning tools. Version 1.2 is the most recent 1EdTech version listed by 1EdTech, with both CSV and REST patterns. [2] It is usually a district, school or vendor procurement requirement rather than a statute. | Implement both CSV import/export and REST 1.2 where feasible; roster users, orgs, courses, classes and enrolments; support role and status changes; gradebook categories, line items, score scales and results; support the Assessment Results Profile; use OAuth/TLS, scoped tokens, pagination, filtering, bulk jobs, retries and reconciliation. Keep source identifiers and deletion/withdrawal semantics. Do not treat a OneRoster resource record as the resource itself: it is metadata used to obtain the resource. |
| **LTI 1.3 and LTI Advantage** | LTI connects a platform/LMS to external tools without a second login. LTI 1.3 improves security using the 1EdTech Security Framework, OAuth 2 and JWTs. LTI Advantage adds Assignment and Grade Services (AGS), Names and Role Provisioning Services (NRPS), and Deep Linking (DL). [3] It is a dominant institutional/RFP expectation in K–12 and higher education. | Act as an LTI 1.3 platform and tool. Implement OIDC login initiation, signed launches, registration, deployment and tool configuration; key rotation and JWKS; least-privilege claims; NRPS roster/role access; AGS line items, scores and results; Deep Linking content selection; launch nonce/state and replay protection; privacy/data-minimisation settings; and per-tool consent/contract records. Treat LTI grades as controlled education-record data, not ordinary telemetry. |
| **Caliper Analytics 1.2** | An 1EdTech event and metric framework for consistently capturing learning activity across resources and platforms. Its profiles cover reading, media, assessment, grading, forum, session, tool-use and related activities. [4] Institutions use it for learning analytics, early warning and outcome analysis. | Implement a Caliper sensor/event pipeline and event store with tenant-configurable retention. Emit profile-valid JSON-LD events with actor, action, object, target, event time, session and organisation/course context; validate vocabulary; deduplicate and replay safely; route to analytics without exposing raw student data to tools by default; document lawful purpose, consent/notice and role access for analytics. |
| **QTI** | Question and Test Interoperability packages and moves assessment items, tests, response processing, usage data and results between authoring, item-bank, delivery and reporting systems. QTI 3.0 combines earlier QTI/APIP work, improves web presentation, supports web components, computer-adaptive testing and portable custom interactions. [5] | Support QTI import/export at the versions buyers need, with an explicit QTI 3.0 roadmap; preserve item metadata, identifiers, scoring logic, outcomes, feedback, media, accessibility alternatives, response variables, item statistics and results. Offer authoring, import, export, import/export and delivery conformance tests. Prevent unsafe custom content, isolate item rendering, and keep answer keys and assessment accommodations access-controlled. |
| **CASE** | Competencies and Academic Standards Exchange provides a REST exchange model for academic standards, competencies, skills, learning outcomes, rubrics and associations. Frameworks and items receive globally unique identifiers so content, assessments, grades and mastery can be aligned across systems. [6] States, boards, districts, curriculum providers and credential systems can be CASE providers or consumers. | Provide CASE provider/consumer APIs; ingest hierarchical frameworks, GUIDs, versions, effective dates, language, jurisdiction and associations; tag courses, lessons, questions, rubrics and results with CASE GUIDs; retain historical mappings when standards change; report mastery by framework item; and link achievements and credentials to competencies. |
| **Open Badges 3.0 and CLR 2.0** | Open Badges 3.0 represents an individual verifiable achievement; CLR 2.0 bundles related achievements into a longitudinal learner record. They are JSON/JSON-LD credentials, cryptographically signed as Verifiable Credentials, and can carry issuer, earner, achievement, criteria, evidence, alignment and endorsements. [7] They are voluntary standards but matter for skills mobility, microcredentials and higher education. | Issue, receive, verify, revoke and export signed OpenBadgeCredential and ClrCredential objects; support VC Data Model 2.0, evidence links, criteria, issuer/earner identifiers, expiration and endorsements; offer learner-initiated wallet transfer and a Badge Connect/OAuth 2 API where required; let learners correct or suppress sharing; keep credential status and key-rotation infrastructure; and avoid embedding unnecessary minors’ personal data in public badge URLs. |
| **Ed-Fi Data Standard** | An open education data model and API ecosystem designed for education agencies, districts and technology providers. Ed-Fi’s own guidance says standardised exchange reduces one-off ETL, exposes combined assessment/attendance data, and improves security by replacing fragile manual/SFTP flows. [8] | Implement an Ed-Fi mapping layer for school, student, staff, course, section, enrolment, attendance, assessment, discipline, program and outcome entities; support API descriptors, namespaces, referential integrity, change/reconciliation jobs, agency-authorised access, and validation against the target Ed-Fi release. Make mappings configurable because state profiles and agency extensions vary. |
| **SIF/A4L** | SIF is an education data-model and infrastructure ecosystem maintained by the Access 4 Learning Community. Its infrastructure is a REST API/transport layer that can carry different data models, support synchronous, asynchronous or hybrid exchange, brokered data hubs, status/error feedback and firewall-friendly cloud integration. A4L also documents Privacy Obligation Document services. [9] | Support SIF infrastructure 3.7/current buyer profile where requested and retain a 3.6 compatibility option when a customer specifies it; implement broker/data-hub patterns, asynchronous queues, message correlation, status/error handling, payload-neutral transport, firewall egress, retry/dead-letter queues and privacy-obligation metadata. Add Australia, New Zealand, UK and North America data-model profiles only when the target market requires them. |
| **CEDS** | Common Education Data Standards is a voluntary US national collaborative data vocabulary and semantic model. The current CEDS pages describe an ontology of entities such as Person, Organisation, Course and Assessment, plus IDS/data-warehouse models for longitudinal P–20W reporting and cloud Parquet. [10] It is not a federal SIS mandate, but is useful for US agency interoperability and data dictionaries. | Map the canonical model to CEDS identifiers, definitions, option sets and relationships; produce a data dictionary and lineage/mapping artefacts; support CEDS IDS/warehouse and Parquet exports where an agency requests them; preserve longitudinal keys and time dimensions; and clearly separate CEDS alignment from legal permission to share data. |
| **xAPI 2.0 and cmi5** | xAPI describes communication about learner activity and experiences between technologies. ADL’s repository notes that the current specification is xAPI 2.0 and separates experience data from processing/validation/security. [11] cmi5 is an xAPI profile for LMS-launched content, specifying launch, authentication, session management, reporting and course structure. [12] They are generally procurement/integration choices, not statutes. | Provide an LRS-compatible xAPI 2.0 endpoint, statement validation, actor/object/verb/context/result/attachments, OAuth or mTLS, tenant isolation, forwarding and retention controls. Implement cmi5 package import, AU/course structure, launch URL and token flow, session state, completion/success/score/duration and xAPI statements. Do not silently turn high-granularity event data into disciplinary or predictive decisions without notice, governance and access controls. |

### Privacy and child-data law

#### US FERPA, COPPA, PPRA and state student-privacy laws

**FERPA.** FERPA is implemented in 34 CFR Part 99 and applies to educational agencies and institutions receiving covered US Department of Education funds. The regulation defines education records as records directly related to a student and maintained by the institution or a party acting for it; it gives parents inspection, amendment and consent rights, transferring to the student at age 18 or attendance at postsecondary education. [13] The “school official” and legitimate educational interest routes do not make a vendor the owner of the data; institutions remain responsible for contract, access, disclosure, redisclosure and recordkeeping decisions.

Product requirements are a role- and purpose-based permission model; parent/eligible-student access and amendment workflows; annual-notice templates and multilingual/accessible delivery; disclosure/redisclosure ledger; export and hold controls; directory-information opt-out; school-official contract metadata; vendor subprocessor register; retention/deletion and legal-hold policies; encryption; and audit logs that can be produced to the institution. The platform should distinguish a minor’s parent from an eligible postsecondary student and support custody/authorisation evidence.

**COPPA, including the 2025 rule.** COPPA applies to operators of child-directed websites/services and operators with actual knowledge that they collect personal information online from children under 13. The FTC rule requires notice, verifiable parental consent, parental review/deletion/control, reasonable security, retention/deletion controls and no conditioning participation on more information than reasonably necessary. [14] The FTC’s April 22, 2025 final rule expanded/clarified definitions and obligations, including mobile telephone, government identifier and biometric identifiers, information security, retention/deletion, notices and consent methods. It expressly did **not** finalise proposed ed-tech school-authorisation provisions while DOE FERPA amendments were pending. [15]

Time-sensitive status: the 2025 amended rule became effective on **23 June 2025**. Regulated entities generally had until **22 April 2026** to comply, except specified provisions in 16 CFR 312.11(d)(1), (d)(4) and (g). [15] As of 27 November 2026, this is an operative rule, not a proposed amendment. Build neutral age-screening for mixed-audience surfaces; parent verification and consent records; child-directed privacy notices; parent review/delete/stop-collection controls; no targeted advertising or unnecessary profiling in school use; retention schedules; security incident evidence; processor/subprocessor controls; and a data inventory that treats biometrics and device/contact data as sensitive.

**PPRA.** The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment gives parents rights concerning certain surveys, inspections and marketing involving students, including inspection of instructional material and policies for covered surveys and collection/use of personal information for marketing. The US Department of Education administers FERPA and PPRA through its Student Privacy Policy Office. [16] Platform implications are configurable survey question-classification and parental-notice/consent workflows, material-access logs, marketing/third-party sharing blocks, district policy publication, and exportable evidence of which students/parents were notified or opted out.

**State laws, including California SOPIPA.** US states add contract, purpose, security, deletion, sale/advertising, profiling and data-breach rules. California’s Student Online Personal Information Protection Act is a baseline example for operators of online services used primarily for K–12 school purposes. [17] A worldwide product should not rely on FERPA alone: maintain a state-law rule engine, prohibit sale/targeted advertising on education data, enforce no secondary commercial use, support district-controlled deletion/return at contract end, subprocessor approval, data security and student/parent rights. Maintain per-state data maps because the population covered, age thresholds, notice, breach and retention requirements differ.

#### EU GDPR, UK GDPR and the UK Age Appropriate Design Code

**EU GDPR.** GDPR is a directly applicable EU regulation for processing personal data in the EU/EEA and for non-EU organisations offering goods/services to or monitoring people there. Its principles include lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality and accountability; it also provides data-subject rights, controller/processor obligations, breach and impact-assessment duties, special-category safeguards and international-transfer rules. The GDPR text is the primary source. [18] Child consent for information-society services is subject to Article 8’s age and Member State variation, so a platform must not hard-code a single global age or assume a school contract resolves every child-data issue.

Use a records-of-processing and data-inventory module; configurable lawful-basis and special-category flags; DPIA templates; controller/processor and subprocessor contracts; data-subject access, correction, restriction, portability and erasure workflows; privacy-by-default settings; breach triage and notification timers; DPO/contact routing; data residency and transfer mechanisms; encryption/key management; minimisation and retention automation; and human review of automated decision/profiling. Separate institutional controller configuration from a vendor processor role.

**UK GDPR and DPA 2018.** The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 provide the UK framework. ICO guidance covers controllers/processors, lawful basis, rights, security, accountability, international transfers and children’s information. [19] A UK deployment therefore needs the same core controls as EU GDPR but should support UK-specific documentation, regulator contacts, transfer risk assessments/IDTA or applicable mechanism, and UK education-sector retention and safeguarding policies.

**UK Age Appropriate Design Code.** The ICO Code is a statutory code of practice for online services likely to be accessed by children; it operationalises the UK GDPR in product design. It sets 15 flexible standards: best interests; DPIA; age-appropriate application; transparency; no detrimental use; policies/community standards; high-privacy defaults; minimisation; sharing; geolocation; parental controls; profiling; nudge techniques; connected devices; and online tools. [20] The product should default child accounts to high privacy, collect the minimum, switch geolocation off, avoid manipulative prompts and child profiling, give age-appropriate notices, expose parental controls without taking away the child’s rights, keep data-sharing purpose-limited, and retain a design/DPIA evidence trail.

#### UK DfE school census and statutory returns

England’s DfE school census guidance is a customer-facing statutory return specification. For 2026–27 it was updated **13 October 2026**, covers autumn 2026 and spring/summer 2027, and states that MIS systems contain the required items even though names and implementation differ. [21] Items include school identifiers and governance, pupils, classes, teachers and support staff, admissions appeals, attendance-related and special-educational-needs data, free-school-meal data, childcare, school time and other modules with collection timing and codes.

A UK MIS connector needs versioned census schemas, code-list validation, collection-period rules, school-phase/governance applicability, pupil/class reconciliation, exception and error messages, audit of source values and changes, XML/CSV or the then-current submission route, and a “generate return” preview with sign-off. Do not treat the DfE census as a generic UK schema: it is England-specific and must be maintained each academic year.

#### Australia Privacy Act

Australia’s Privacy Act 1988 regulates Australian Government agencies and organisations above the relevant turnover threshold, with exceptions and additional covered entities. It contains 13 Australian Privacy Principles governing collection, notice, use/disclosure, quality, security, access/correction and cross-border handling. [22] An education platform should support APP privacy notices, purpose limitation, access/correction, secure deletion, cross-border disclosure and supplier controls, data-quality workflows, privacy impact assessments, incident response and the Notifiable Data Breaches process.

Time-sensitive child-data note: the 2024 Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act mandated an OAIC Children’s Online Privacy Code. OAIC’s page, updated **5 August 2026**, says the Code applies to covered online services likely to be accessed by children or primarily concerned with children’s activities and must be finalised/registered by **10 December 2026**. [23] Treat this as an active implementation deadline on the as-of date, not as a completed final code; design for high privacy, age-appropriate transparency, minimisation, child-centred risk assessment and no unnecessary profiling while monitoring the final instrument.

### India: privacy, policy and education DPI

#### Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and Rules 2025

The DPDP Act defines a **child** as an individual who has not completed 18 years, applies to processing in India and to offshore processing connected with offering goods/services to people in India, and makes a Data Fiduciary responsible for processing done by it or its Data Processor. The Act requires lawful purpose, notice, consent or certain legitimate uses, purpose-limited data, reasonable security safeguards, breach intimation, erasure when the purpose is no longer served unless law requires retention, contact information and grievance redressal. [24]

For children, the Act requires verifiable parental consent before processing child personal data and prohibits tracking or behavioural monitoring of children and targeted advertising directed at children, subject to statutory exceptions. It also gives the Central Government power to notify Significant Data Fiduciaries with additional duties. Build age/child-status and guardian relationship records, parent-verification evidence, consent notices in English or an Eighth Schedule language, withdrawal propagation to processors, a consent ledger, purpose/field minimisation, child-safe defaults, no behavioural advertising, rights requests, grievance handling and deletion/retention orchestration.

The government notified the DPDP Rules 2025 on **14 November 2025**. The official phased commencement is important: Rules 1, 2 and 17–21 commenced on publication; Rule 4 commenced one year later; Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23 commence 18 months after publication. [25] Therefore, as of 27 November 2026, Rule 4 is in force and the detailed child-consent, security, breach, retention and rights mechanisms in Rules 3 and 5–16 are scheduled for the 18-month date in May 2027, unless a later notification changes that position. A product may implement them early, but must not mislabel future provisions as already operative.

Rule 10 specifies verifiable parental consent and reasonable diligence to establish that the consenting person is an identifiable adult, using reliable identity/age information or voluntarily provided information/token from an authorised entity, including a Digital Locker service provider. [25] Build an abstraction layer so verification can use institution-held adult evidence, an authorised identity/age token or DigiLocker-linked flow without unnecessarily storing the parent’s identity document. Rule 6 of the notified Rules describes encryption, masking/tokenisation, access control, logs/monitoring/review, backup/continuity, processor contract safeguards and organisational measures; Rule 7 requires prompt individual notice and Board reporting, with a 72-hour update/detail window stated in the text. [25]

The Act’s maximum penalty for failure to take reasonable security safeguards is up to **₹250 crore**; breach-notification and child-obligation contraventions can reach **₹200 crore**, and other listed contraventions can reach **₹50 crore**. These are statutory maximums, not automatic fines. [26] Build an evidence pack: records of processing, consent and notices, processor contracts, access/log reviews, security testing, backup/restore tests, incident timeline, Board/individual notices, rights tickets and deletion proofs.

#### NEP 2020 and the architecture direction

NEP 2020 is the policy context for competency-based, multidisciplinary, flexible and technology-enabled education. The operational product consequence is not one NEP API. It is a need for stage/grade flexibility, multilingual and inclusive content, competency/outcome tracking, formative and holistic assessment, vocational and higher-education pathways, credit mobility, teacher development and data-informed improvement. DIKSHA’s current portal reflects NEP stage structure from Foundational through Secondary and supports board/state tenants, textbooks, video, interactive content, courses and accessibility settings. [27]

#### UDISE+

UDISE+ is India’s Ministry of Education school-education data platform. Its current portal provides school search, dashboards, archives, microdata requests, GIS, PGI, a data-sharing portal, a developer portal, data-capture formats and 2025–26 reports; the notice board shows AY 2026–27 data completion. [28] The product needs a UDISE+ reporting adapter with UDISE codes, school/teacher/student/class/programme/facility and outcome data, versioned data-capture formats, validation, role-based state/district/school views, submission status and reconciliation. Keep UDISE reporting separate from the operational canonical record so corrections and source ownership are explicit.

#### APAAR ID, Academic Bank of Credits, DigiLocker and NAD

APAAR is the “One Nation, One Student ID” Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry. Its official portal says parents submit voluntary consent for minors; UDISE generates APAAR against the student’s PEN; the ID is pushed into DigiLocker; and the 12-digit identifier links academic credits, marksheets, degrees, diplomas, certificates and co-curricular accomplishments. [29] The platform must treat APAAR as an external identifier, not as a replacement for local IDs: store consent and provenance, support duplicate/mismatch resolution, never expose it unnecessarily, and make joins reversible and auditable.

ABC is the Ministry of Education’s Academic Bank of Credits, regulated by UGC and developed/maintained by Digital India Corporation. The official portal describes secure storage, accumulation, transfer and redemption of credits from recognised institutions, integrated with APAAR, DigiLocker and NAD, and provides an API directory. [30] Implement course/credit structures, academic terms, outcomes, transfer/redemption status, awarding-institution authority, APAAR linkage, signed record packages, learner consent, DigiLocker/NAD delivery and correction/revocation workflows. The record model should handle formal, vocational and recognised non-academic learning.

#### DIKSHA

DIKSHA is a national school-education digital platform linked from the Ministry/NCERT ecosystem. The portal supports NCERT, CBSE, NIOS and state/UT tenants; NEP stages; multilingual resources; QR-linked textbooks; courses, virtual labs and teacher/student content; and accessibility options such as text-to-speech, text size, line-height, link highlighting, dyslexia-friendly display and hide-images mode. [27] Integrate through documented APIs/tenant contracts rather than scraping. Support content/resource IDs, board, medium, grade, subject, language, licensing, accessibility metadata, progress/credential exchange and offline/mobile constraints.

#### PARAKH Holistic Progress Card

PARAKH/NCERT’s Holistic Progress Cards implement the NEP shift from rote knowledge acquisition to competency-based and holistic assessment. The HPC covers Foundational, Preparatory, Middle and Secondary stages and captures performance across curricular elements and multidisciplinary activities. [31] A platform should model competency evidence, teacher/self/peer/parent feedback where used, activities, rubrics, developmental narratives, stage transitions, languages and generated cards. Support a digital HPC export/import and preserve the underlying evidence rather than only a rendered PDF.

#### CBSE and state-board requirements

Boards are not one national API. CBSE, NIOS and each state board can differ in registration, candidate data, subject/combination codes, examination forms, internal assessment, attendance, practicals, results, migration/transfer certificates, correction windows, language and submission calendars. DIKSHA’s explicit board/state tenant structure illustrates this variation. [27] Use a board-adapter registry, versioned code lists, bulk file/API exchange, field-level validation, approval and correction workflow, digital-signature/evidence storage, and configurable retention. Never hard-code CBSE fields as universal Indian education fields.

#### NAAC, binary accreditation and AQAR

NAAC is an autonomous UGC institution for assessment and accreditation of higher-education institutions. Its current site exposes HEI/assessor portals, assessment/accreditation processes, criteria and weightages, AQAR and IQAC workflows. [32] NAAC’s reform notice records a move toward **Binary Accreditation** followed by Maturity Based Graded Levels; it also states transition rules for institutions with pending or valid RAF applications. [32] As of November 2026, implement both legacy RAF-grade evidence and the new binary/maturity evidence model, with a configurable versioned self-study repository.

Product features include criterion/metric evidence, programme and institution scope, IQAC actions, AQAR cycles, document/version/approver workflow, faculty/publication/infrastructure/student-outcome data, survey evidence, data lineage, assessor access and immutable submission packs. Keep accreditation evidence distinct from operational analytics and provide institution-controlled export.

#### NBA

The National Board of Accreditation accredits programmes, especially engineering and other professional programmes, using an online Accreditation Workflow Management System; its site provides accreditation, application and accredited-programme workflows and a new Self-Assessment Report for UG Engineering Tier I. [33] Build programme-level outcome-based education entities: programme educational objectives, graduate attributes, course outcomes, CO–PO/PSO mappings, attainment calculations, assessment evidence, faculty, facilities, continuous-improvement actions and SAR export. Support tier/discipline/version-specific templates and evidence locks.

#### NIRF

NIRF is the Ministry of Education’s National Institutional Ranking Framework, launched in 2015. Its parameters include Teaching, Learning and Resources; Research and Professional Practice; Graduation Outcomes; Outreach and Inclusivity; and Perception. [34] A university platform should maintain the denominator definitions, academic-year snapshots and evidence for faculty, students, research, sponsored projects, patents/publications, placement/graduation outcomes, finance, diversity and outreach. Provide a reviewable NIRF data mart and data dictionary rather than a one-click “ranking score” with no lineage.

#### AISHE

AISHE is an annual web-based Ministry of Education survey covering higher-education institutions and collecting teachers, enrolment, programmes, examination results, finance and infrastructure. The portal states that the 2025–26 survey is open and points to institution registration, web DCF and 2023–24 reports. [35] Implement AISHE code and institution master, year-specific DCF schemas, programme/teacher/student/finance/infrastructure fields, validation and approval, submission status and export. Treat AISHE as a reporting snapshot, not the authoritative live student record.

#### Samarth eGov university ERP

Samarth is an Indian higher-education digital-campus/ERP ecosystem used for admissions, student and faculty workflows, examinations, internal assessment, administration and related university services. Its official site provides capability guides for admin, faculty and students and records deployments for admissions and data management across universities/colleges. [36] For interoperability, expose modular APIs and import/export for institution, programme, applicant, admission, fee, course, registration, attendance, internal/practical marks, examination, results, transcripts, faculty/staff, finance and reporting. Support university/state tenancy, workflow configuration, Indian languages, Aadhaar/APAAR/DigiLocker/ABC as optional external services, and clean migration from existing Samarth deployments.

### Accessibility

| Framework | Who requires or uses it | Product implications |
|---|---|---|
| **WCAG 2.2** | W3C’s current Web Content Accessibility Guidelines cover web content and user agents; WCAG 2.2 was published as a W3C Recommendation in 2023 and adds/updates success criteria. [37] It is the common technical baseline behind many laws and procurement requirements. | Target WCAG 2.2 AA for web/mobile web and document outputs. Implement semantic HTML, keyboard/focus order, visible focus, skip links, labels/errors, contrast, reflow/zoom, captions/transcripts, audio description where needed, non-colour status, accessible authentication, target size, drag alternatives, reduced motion, screen-reader names, accessible tables/forms and accessible PDFs/exports. Test automated plus keyboard, screen reader, zoom, low vision, cognitive and mobile workflows. Publish an accessibility statement and issue log. |
| **US Section 508** | Revised Section 508 applies to covered US federal agencies and their electronic content/ICT, incorporating WCAG 2.0 Level AA by reference and covering web, documents, software, native mobile apps and authoring tools. [38] A school vendor may face it through federal procurement or funded programmes. | Provide an Accessibility Conformance Report/VPAT mapped to the applicable 508/WCAG criteria; ensure native apps, PDFs, authoring tools and third-party components are covered; retain test evidence and a remedial roadmap. Do not claim 508 merely because the main website passes. |
| **EN 301 549** | The European ICT accessibility standard covers websites, mobile apps, software, hardware and documents and closely follows WCAG. ETSI’s current reference is EN 301 549 v3.2.1 aligned closely to WCAG 2.1 AA. [39] It is a key procurement/accessibility benchmark in Europe. | Test full ICT lifecycle, including mobile apps, documents, authentication, support, authoring, video and hardware integrations. Map to EN 301 549 clauses, keep an EU accessibility conformance statement, support assistive technologies and provide accessible procurement evidence. |
| **India GIGW 3.0** | Guidelines for Indian Government Websites are India’s government web quality, accessibility, usability, security and governance guidance. The official portal lists GIGW Manual 3.0, accessibility/tools, semantic markup, accessible forms and STQC certification routes; it was updated 25 November 2026. [40] Government deployments and public-facing education services should follow it. | Use semantic markup, accessible forms/alt text, screen-reader and keyboard support, mobile friendliness, valid HTML/CSS, broken-link checks, multilingual content, privacy/security/website policies, feedback and grievance routes, metadata, uptime/monitoring and audit/certification evidence. |

### Security and assurance

**SOC 2.** SOC 2 is an AICPA CPA-attestation service/report over controls relevant to Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality and/or Privacy; it is not a product security certification or a law. AICPA describes SOC as a suite of assurance reports used by users to assess outsourcing risk. [41] A commercial SaaS platform should maintain a control matrix, system description, risk assessment, logical/physical access, change management, vulnerability/incident response, backup/DR, vendor management, privacy and evidence collection suitable for a Type 2 report. Make the report scope, period, exceptions and subservice organisations explicit.

**ISO/IEC 27001:2022.** ISO/IEC 27001:2022 specifies requirements for an information security management system. It is an international, certifiable management-system standard covering risk management, confidentiality, integrity and availability; certification is optional but widely used in procurement. [42] Build an ISMS around asset/data inventory, risk register, statement of applicability, policies, access reviews, secure development, supplier/cloud controls, incident management, business continuity, internal audit, management review and corrective actions. Align the open-source project’s contribution and release process with secure SDLC, dependency governance and vulnerability disclosure.

**OWASP ASVS 5.0.** ASVS is an open application-security verification standard for designing, developing and testing web applications and services. Version **5.0.0 was published 30 May 2025**; its requirements provide a metric, guidance and procurement baseline. [43] Use versioned ASVS IDs in acceptance criteria. Cover architecture, encoding/injection prevention, validation, authentication, session management, access control, cryptography, error handling/logging, data protection, communications, malicious code, business logic, files, configuration and API security. Add automated SAST/DAST/dependency/container scans, threat modelling, penetration testing, fuzzing, secrets detection, SBOM/provenance and reproducible builds.

### Implementation priorities

1. **Core trust layer:** canonical model, external IDs, purpose/consent/guardian records, data classification, retention/deletion, rights/grievance workflows, encryption, tenant isolation, audit ledger, backups and incident response.
2. **Global interoperability:** OneRoster CSV/REST, LTI 1.3 Advantage, QTI, Caliper, CASE, Open Badges/CLR, xAPI/cmi5; then Ed-Fi/CEDS/SIF adapters where target buyers require them.
3. **India pack:** UDISE+ schemas and API/data-capture connector; APAAR/PEN/DigiLocker consent and mismatch handling; ABC/NAD credit and award exchange; DIKSHA content/tenant integration; PARAKH HPC; board-adapter registry; AISHE/NIRF/NAAC/NBA evidence and reports; Samarth migration/API pack.
4. **Accessibility and assurance:** WCAG 2.2 AA design system, EN 301 549/Section 508/GIGW mappings, accessible document generation, ASVS-based secure SDLC, ISO 27001 ISMS and SOC 2 evidence readiness.
5. **Jurisdiction operations:** release calendars and schemas for DfE census, US state laws and contracts, EU/UK transfer and child-code rules, Australian APP/NDB and Children’s Online Privacy Code, and India’s DPDP commencement/Rules updates. Date every legal/configuration pack and expose a customer-facing change log.

The strategic conclusion is that worldwide saleability is less about supporting every acronym in one database than about providing a stable canonical record, versioned conformance adapters, explicit consent and provenance, accessible interfaces, and evidence that a school or university can export, correct, delete, audit and govern its data without vendor lock-in.
